doc.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022

title: Explaining the clave and finding the one
summary: Clave never changes, the phrase does; conga patterns; why outsiders lose beat one and his own early confusion.

bands.name: Alex Torres and the Latin Kings

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I’m fascinated sometimes why a 3-2 clave is played instead of a 2-3 clave. Can you enlighten me?

Okay. Once the song starts the clave never changes. The phrase changes. And I’ll give you a good example. Let me — I’ve got to — here we go. Remember that advertisement for Chiquita Banana [sings] Chiquita Banana and I come to say? Okay. You’re going to notice at the end of that phrase I’m going to be clapping the clave. The clave doesn’t change but the phrase changes. [scats and claps] Three two. Two three. See what I mean?
And once the clave begins it never changes. It’s the phrase that changes, that goes along with the clave.
That’s how I needed it to be explained.

Yeah. And by the way, that also, the clave is the basis of how the conga player plays, because he’ll play two three [scats] boom boom. That boom boom is on the one, two, three. [Scats] So it all hooks up.

It all hooks up. I used to have a job booking groups for public school performances and one year we had this marvelous Latin band from Albany, Alex Torres and the Latin Kings. And they had the three percussionists and horns and piano and I remember getting, I guess aggravated with myself because they would get going and I would lose beat one. And I thought I was a pretty educated musician.

That’s not unusual. That’s a common thing for people who are not raised in that culture and are used to hearing it all the time, the same way somebody in a Latin community would listen to a blues and not know where does it start? Well you know where it starts because you can hear where it starts. But they’re not used to hearing it that way. So that’s not an uncommon thing. Like I said, when I first started learning about it, boy that bass part really threw me off and I had the same question, where is the one? As a matter of fact guys made little jokes about it ‘cause some have written songs, “Where’s the One.” You know when you get deeper into the rhythms and you get into the Cuban group, there’s a group called [Los] Muñuquitos de Matanzas, which is just a drums and vocal group, that’s all. Just a bunch of drummers, all conga players, maybe someone playing the cowbell. When you hear that you can get lost easily. Where is the one? When you want to go deeper than that you get into more African rhythms where again, you know, you can be surprised, where is the one? How come I lost it, I was following it so carefully. But it’s really just a matter of listening and listening. Like I said the fellow Frankie Malabé who was an inspiration to me, was the one who took me down that road of starting me off listening to Tito Puente and Tito Rodriguez and Machito, because he knew that I could understand where the beat was and what was going on. Then we’d go a little bit deeper into the drumming and voices groups and after I thought that I had it down listening to Puente and Machito, all of a sudden I was back to square one. Where’s the one? So that’s a very interesting journey to take.
